source.title: Eligibility Traces and Plasticity on Behavioral Time Scales: Experimental Support of NeoHebbian Three-Factor Learning Rules.

confidence_rationale: Authoritative review of the theory and the key experiments behind three-factor rules (local eligibility x global neuromodulator). Supports MECH-452's framing, but as a review it adds framework rather than new evidence, and it does not address loop-organised locality.
failure_signatures: The review establishes that eligibility is synapse-local and the third factor broadcast; it does not argue that eligibility must be partitioned by cortico-BG loop.
Its time-scale argument (traces bridging ms spikes to seconds of behaviour) implies a trace that is too SHORT also fails credit assignment, a symmetric failure mode MECH-452's text does not name.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Co-activation of pre- and postsynaptic neurons sets a synaptic eligibility flag that yields a weight change only if a third factor (a neuromodulator signalling reward, punishment, surprise or novelty) arrives while the flag is set; four key experiments now support such traces on behavioural (seconds) time scales.
mapping.ree_translation: The general computational form MECH-452 instantiates: effective update = broadcast third factor x local eligibility x recent co-activity. Positions REE's per-loop eligibility buffers as a coarse-grained three-factor rule and gives the vocabulary for the claim's collapse-to-global ablation (removing locality of the eligibility term while keeping the third factor fixed).
mapping.mapping_caveat: A review: it adds framework and a curated reading of evidence rather than an independent finding. It treats the third factor as potentially multiple neuromodulators, which is broader than REE's single ARC-108 delta_t; and it is silent on loop-level organisation.
mapping.source_context: Review of theory and of experimental work in striatum, hippocampus and cortex (including Yagishita 2014 and related studies).

confidence_components.notes: Well-cited review by a leading theory group; confidence capped because it is framework, not new evidence.
